text: Welcome, investors, to the Absolute Return Podcast, your source for stock market analysis,
global macro musings, and hedge fund investment strategies. Your hosts, Julian Clamajko and
Michael Kesslering aim to bring you the knowledge and analysis you need to become a more intelligent
and wealthier investor. This episode is brought to you by Accelerate Financial Technologies.
Accelerate because performance matters. Find out more at AccelerateShares.com.
Hey, everyone. Welcome to the Absolute Return Podcast. On today's show, we welcome special
guest, Victory Capital's Chairman and CEO, David Brown. Victory Capital is a diversified
global investment management firm offering a wide array of independent investment approaches
and innovative solutions. On the show, we discuss the multi-boutique model and the competitive
advantage it provides, the firm's approach to mergers and acquisitions, where the biggest
opportunities for growth are in the investment management industry, his advice for the next
generation of business leaders, and more. With no further ado, here's our show on building
a modern asset management platform with Victory Capital's Chairman and CEO, David Brown.
I'm pleased to welcome David from Victory Capital onto the show. How are you doing today, David?
Good. Thanks for having me.
Excited to get into Victory Capital's business model. It's such an interesting industry,
and you've been with Victory Capital since 2004, and investment management has really
evolved dramatically over the past 22 years. From your perspective, moving to leadership
at the firm as chairman and CEO, how has that journey been since when you joined the industry
way back when to now? The industry has changed a lot, and I feel like it's going under a lot
of change right now as well. I've actually been in the industry since actually the mid-90s.
My perspective even goes back further than 2004, but from an industry and from our business,
so much has changed. I think about the mid-2000s, and it was really before ETFs
were really available. I think most of the investable assets were in active management.
We were just starting to see passive start to take shape. Then also really from a distribution
side, two decades ago, how you accessed, at least for us, US intermediary clients,
how you dealt with the large platforms. From an institutional perspective, consultants were
really just starting to come into shape here, at least in the US, where most of the large
organizations were just starting to use consultants and look at consultants to help them with their
asset allocation, portfolios. So much has changed, but for our business, two decades ago, we were
owned by Keycorp. We're owned by Regional Bank, actually out of Cleveland, Ohio. We went through
the financial crisis, which I think changed the whole financial industry and the landscape,
and specifically, investor management. That was really the beginning of us thinking about
how we would get our business outside of Keybank and really get into a situation where we thought
we could serve our clients better. Going back, at least from our perspective and our business,
we bought our business out from Keycorp in 2013. The employees, a group of employees,
about 120 employees, and then we partnered with a private equity firm, Crestview. We started our
journey in July of 2013. The industry was going through a lot of change. I think, at that point,
ASEV was really starting to take shape. There was a debate on whether active equities and
active-made sense in portfolios. Over the last, I think it'll be 13 years in June or July. Since
then, we've done a number of acquisitions. We've totally reshaped our business. I guess we'll talk
about our business model, but we've fully rounded out our business model. I would also say, over
the last two decades, outside of our business changing a lot, I think technology has changed as
well. How portfolio managers build portfolios, how they use technology, how they use data. I think,
decades ago, people were looking at spreadsheets. They were getting data on paper and the
speed of the data was so slow compared to what we have now. One of the advantages is, if you had
access to data, in today's world, I think one of the advantages is, do you know how to sort through
all of the data to get to the data that you need and that's most effective? That whole cycle of
how that has evolved has just been fascinating. What I also find fascinating is just the change
in ownership over the years. You went from being owned by a regional bank, then private equity,
and now a public company. Was there any change in strategy and the direction of the business
under various ownership structures? When we were owned by eBank in my early years,
we were employees. We had no ownership in victory capital. The strategy of the business
was different. The business was totally different. We were truly, I would say, the investment arm
of eBank, of a bank. A lot of our clients were associated with KeyCorp. We had a truly independent
retail business, but a lot of them were associated with KeyCorp. We were doing a lot of different
things. We had a securities lending business. We had a custody business. We had a fixed income
business, money market business, an equity business. It was highly complicated. We're doing a lot of
things to a lot of people. When we bought our business out in 2013, we really created the
foundation and the strategy that we have today. It was a version of the multi-botique. We're
actually more of an integrated firm than a multi-botique, but it was really the foundation
of the strategy that we're still executing today. At that point, we were majority owned by a private
equity firm, and the employees had sizable ownership. At that point, the employees owned
about a third of the business, and private equity owned about two-thirds of the business.
The strategy at that point was set, and I would say today, we still have generally the same
strategy we had 13 years ago when we came into a dependent company. We're employee-owned. We feel
employee-led, and really, we've tried to create this environment where we have shareholders,
and we had this 13 years ago. We have shareholders, we have clients, and we have employees
all on the same level, and all just as important. You hear a lot of leaders talk about, oh, my most
important circle is my employees, or my most important circle are my clients. We've actually
taken the approach that all of them are equal, and they all have to be in balance to create a
long-term business, and a viable business is going to last. If you have your shareholders that all
you care about, and that's at the expense of your clients and your employees, you probably are not
going to have a good business. On the other side, if all you care about is your clients, and you
forget about your shareholders, and you forget about your employees, you're not going to have a
long-standing business. That's been a core foundation of what we've done. Part of that,
that strategy is we have high employee ownership of our stock, and we have high employee ownership
of our products. We're one of the few traditional asset management firms that actually publish
in our annual report what our employees own of our stock, or of our products. We have a little
over 700 employees at the end of 2025. Those 700-plus employees own $350 million of our products all by
choice. If you think about it, the shareholders, because they own our stock, we have clients,
and then we have employees, and our employees go in all three of those circles. It creates a really
good culture, and a really good culture where you put clients at the forefront, you put employees
at the forefront, and then obviously shareholders. Eating your own cooking, so to speak, and perhaps
that's one of the keys to success. I did want to get into the details of your unique business model
that integrated or multi-boutique approach. Could you discuss how that came to be, and have you
viewed the competitive advantage of that model versus the traditional asset management?
It's very unique. When we did our MBO in 2013, we really were trying to solve
for one issue and something that we thought was super important. It really goes like this. In our
business, we think the best way to manage clients' portfolios is to have active, dedicated teams.
The concept of let's get seven people in a garage with some bloombergs and facset,
and go manage money, and that's all they do. We think that that is a real advantage to eliminate
all the other distractions that sometimes portfolio managers, when they go to construct
portfolios, have. Let's see if we can do that. The other side of it is understanding, and we knew
this a while ago, that you're going to have to have a sizable distribution, best-of-class
operations technology, administrative platform, if you're going to be able to convince clients
of size to allocate dollars to. How do you thread that needle? That's what we were trying to solve.
What we did is we created a business model that we call the next version of a multi-boutique
and really next generation. For us, this business, this platform that we have works like this. We
have franchises that have their own brand, and they have investment autonomy. We have eight of
them today, Sycamore, Trivale, and RS, and they have their own brand, their own logo, their own
identity, and they all manage money differently. They don't share research, they create their own
research, create their own portfolio, and they all have their own edge. Most of them have their
own offices and are working sitting in their own area, and they have their own mini-culture,
and that's what we're promoting. But those franchises and those brands are not separate
companies. They are not separate registered investment advisors in the US. They don't have
their separate administrative operations or distribution platforms. They're leveraging
a platform. That's the other side of it, is they leverage one platform with size, with scale,
with expertise, and those things that they're leveraging, they're getting the best of both
worlds. A client is getting independent, autonomous, almost boutique investment management sitting on
a size and scale platform that's not complicated, that eliminates all of the burden, the administrative
burden, and the distribution burden to the investment teams. Those investment franchises
plug into a very sizable and scale distribution. Our distribution is outside the US, inside the US,
US intermediary, US institutional, we have a direct business, and they plug into all of those things.
All they have to do is manage money, go out, help us interact with clients, help us service
clients, and that's all they have to do. We eliminate all of that. Our business model is very
scaled, very simple. We like this concept of one. We have one trading platform. We have one
compliance system. We have one technology platform. It becomes very scalable. You can invest in it in
a really efficient way. It actually becomes very conducive to acquisitions as well, because what
lined up happening when you want to go out and buy businesses to expand your product set is
you get all the investment talent, you don't disrupt that, you actually promote that, and then
everything else you get to bring onto your platform and eliminate your duplication.
That's our model. If you looked at the traditional multi-boutique in the US and looked at the
traditional firm, most of them fall into the integrated side. If you think about BlackRock,
fully integrated. You were to look at like an AMG here in the US, a public company,
as multi-boutique as you can get. Separate platforms, they have a holding company.
We're really the best of both of those, more leaning toward an integrated business.
There's just a tremendous amount of synergies when you speak about distribution and sales and
compliance and all that. Certainly, that integrated model makes sense. Now, you mentioned M&A,
so making acquisitions and kind of bolting them onto your platform. Can you discuss industry,
consolidation opportunities in general, and also Victory Capital's approach to M&A?
Yeah. We have an unbelievably fragmented industry. If you think about a comparison to banks here in
the US, there is an unbelievable number of banks and there is an unbelievable number of
investment management firms. Our industry has really begun to consolidate. You can see there's
been a lot of transactions. My opinion is it's going to increase in intensity as we go forward.
The reason is that size and scale matter. You're going to need a size distribution force to get
the clients. You're going to need lots of investment dollars to go and invest in your
operations, your technology, the AI to stay current and to buy data and to get data and the
source data and the sort data. Then the buyers of our products specifically on the US intermediary
side are doing business with less firms. Those would be the Merrill Lynch's, the UBS's,
the Morgan Stanley's. They're doing business with less firms. They're requiring those firms
to invest a lot more money in their platforms. Marketing, premier partnerships, buying data,
conferences, collateral, all of those things, the bar is going up. Then you have to have a wide enough
and deep enough product set to square off with these platforms because they're doing business with
less firms. Those firms they do business with better have a complete product set.
The size and scale needed just in that part of our industry is massive and only growing.
Then in addition, the value add an investment manager really is bringing the clients as the
investment management piece. It isn't the middle and back office. It isn't the settlement or the
reconciliation of accounts. A lot of that can be done almost from a perspective of it doesn't
matter who does that. If you think about those dynamics where I need to get bigger, be able to
square off, and some of the things I do outside of investment management I can have someone else do,
it really does push towards consolidation. You're seeing the big get bigger. Actually,
you're seeing the firms in the middle have to make a choice either they need to get bigger or
they need to get smaller and become very specialized. The middle will not survive a decade out.
They will be consolidated away. They'll be in a business that's shrinking, but it'll really be
that middle. I'd say middle is probably $100 billion to $700 or $800 billion, $100 billion to
$700 or $800 billion. It's a wide area. Where we are today, we're in the middle and we have
aspirations to get the other side. I always talk about is there's two islands. There's a small
island is the big island. We're in the water and we're on a speedboat to the big island,
but we got to get there. We have time, but we have to get there. Since we became an independent
company, 12 and a half years ago, we've done eight acquisitions. We've grown our assets from
about $15 billion to well over $300 billion today. We've publicly said our aspirations
are to be a trillion-dollar manager. I'd love to get there through organic growth.
I think that's highly unlikely given the industry dynamics. We'll get there through
organic growth, but we'll also get there through acquisitions. I talked about our platform earlier
being really conducive to acquisitions. What I mean by that is a lot of the acquisitions that
our industry have failed as they try to put investment teams and talent together. I've
never understood that. I've always thought you buy an investment team that's doing well.
Why would you want to disrupt what they're doing and try to do something different? Our model,
our platform, is preserve the investment talent as is, give them more resources than they have
today, give them all the resources they need, take away all of the distractions, plug them into the
best of class ops, technology, data, and plug them into a really good big distribution system.
When we buy businesses, we do that. Then there's a lot of other things in investment management,
business distribution, marketing, operations, technology. We then enlarge our platform and
bring some of those people on and some of those resources on, but there is duplications. There
turns out to be an ability to grow your platform, but there's also an opportunity to
have cost synergies. We call them net expense synergies, which turn out to be really good
from an accretion standpoint on earnings. We'll be a big participant in consolidation.
It's part of who we are. It's part of our business. It's actually part of our skill set.
We've created a lot of choices for our clients from a product perspective. We have
pretty much from a public market offering products in every asset class, almost in every
geography from an investment perspective, also on fixed income as well, not just equities. Then
we've also created a really scale distribution infrastructure. We have clients in 60 countries
in addition to the US. Then we've created a lot of value for our shareholders
since we did our MBO and surely since we've gone public. I know we're the best performing
traditional asset manager by far from a total shareholder return perspective for our stock,
BCTR. You mentioned on the M&A strategy, cost synergies are really important, but
on the back end of M&A, going from estimated to realized synergies is really
difficult historically for acquirers. You've been able to take those from estimated to realized
and actually achieve those synergy goals. What would you say differentiates your team
as operators in your ability to do exactly that at post-acquisition?
We are really unique in that sense. It's not just one thing. A couple unique things about us
is we don't have an M&A team. We've done all this M&A acquisitions and we don't have an M&A team.
Our team, our managers and our leaders do all of the diligence. They do all of the integration
plans. They do all the negotiation. They do the closing and then they do all of the actual
integration to realization. They build the plans and then they see them through to the end and
they're responsible. We don't use consultants. A lot of times, not only do you lose the knowledge
when the consultant leaves, but the plans are not the people executing. That's one thing.
If you do that enough times and we've done it eight times, you get better at those things.
You make mistakes. You learn from them. You get better. There's a real expertise. I've said on
a public call that we're actually in two businesses. We're in the investment management
business and we're in the acquisition business. I would submit to you that there's a lot of
investment managers that want to do acquisitions and then there's investment managers and then
there's acquirers and that's who we are. It's subtle, but it's different. I think that's one
thing. I also think we had a real chance to start with a blank piece of paper in 2013 when we did our
management buyout. We bought the pieces of the business that we wanted. We started with a blank,
clean piece of paper with no legacy issues. Very few times in business, do you get that chance?
We did it. Then along the way, we were very committed to lack of complexity, simplicity,
and building the business the right way, brick by brick, very simply. We didn't do one-offs.
We didn't change our structure here to just get this deal done. We were very committed to the
structure we have, which is no investment franchise has on franchise distribution. No
investment franchise, they all are compensated the same structure. We use a revenue share.
We didn't do any one-offs, which makes it very easy down the road if people are willing to commit
to your business model to integrate them in. Pretty good at work experience. I think we have
good people. The other last thing I would say is we have stuck to things that we are good at.
We've not chased the hot dot. We have stayed to be a traditional asset manager. In the asset
classes, we know we've become experts in those asset classes, and we haven't ventured out in
areas where maybe we're not as good or the platform wouldn't support it or we just were in
experience, so we've stuck to our dating, if you will. With that, I'm curious as to where you see
the next growth opportunities. You've obviously executed this playbook for a decade plus.
The future going to bring just more of the same sort of traditional bolt-on acquisitions, or do
you guys explore new asset classes or private markets or alternatives? Where do you see the main
growth opportunities for the firm in the next five to ten years?
The industry, we talked about earlier, the industry is evolving. The way we look at it is
we've evolved our product set, our vehicles, how we distribute, how we interact with our clients.
I think ETFs for us are Victory Share's platform, which we bought into that business
2015, so over 10 years ago, had $200 million, and today we're approaching $20 billion.
I see ETFs as a big part of our future, and it's integrated into our distribution and kind of our
ecosystem, and our clients, advisors are inside the US, outside the US. That's an area that they
want to buy from us. ETFs, I think SMAs and models are going to be a big part of our growth.
We have two fixed income franchises. We're seeing a lot of demand there. I think fixed income,
with what's happening here in the US with demographics, aging, and I'm a big believer in
active management and fixed income. If you look at the benchmarks and fixed income,
they're very hard to just say, I want to buy the benchmark. So many names in most of these
benchmarks. I think fixed income will be a big driver for us, multi-asset, which is part of one
of our franchises, plus our solutions platform. I also think active equities done right, packaged
right, so either in an active ETF. An ETF is a share class in a mutual fund. It's an SMA,
maybe with a tax-efficient wrapper, so that I think they will do very well as well, and we'll
participate in all of that. Then a big growth driver for us, which we're really just beginning
the journey on, is outside the US. We have about $55 billion outside the US. I guess we're in 60
countries. That distribution comes to us through the Amundi distribution partnership arrangement
we have. Basically, that works. Just for information, Amundi is close to a $3 trillion
manager. I think it's a top 10 manager in the world. We bought in, we closed in April of 25.
We bought their US manufacturing, our basic pioneer investments here in the US. We bought that
business, and part of that transaction is we issued them some ownership in our company,
gave them two board seats. But most importantly, from an outside the US, we have an exclusive
distribution arrangement where they are required. They can only sell our products. Anything is
traditional asset management that is manufactured in the US, and they sell that outside the US has
to be off our platform. We have this massive distribution force around in Europe, in Asia,
in different parts of the world, selling our products. That's a huge growth driver for us.
The pioneer franchises, which is what we bought, is already in that system, and we're seeing flows
there. One of the big opportunities, the legacy victory products that was not part of pioneer
before or Amundi before, is just getting put in that system. That's going to be a big growth driver
as well. USIT's institutional mandates. What's really fascinating is the US is at a certain
point in its life cycle in the investment management industry. Not everywhere in the world is in that
life cycle. Some are 20 years behind. Some are 10 years behind. Some of the tax structures are
different. The fees are different. Some of the challenges in the US are not challenges outside
the US. We have some challenges outside the US that aren't in the US, but it's a really good
piece for us, and it's a big growth driver for us as well.
You described the Amundi relationship. That's certainly something that is unique and differentiated
for your distribution platform and growth opportunities outside the US. Can you provide a
little bit more detail outside of that? What else would you say really makes your distribution
platform unique? That's obviously been a big selling feature in terms of bringing on some of
these new asset managers through acquisition. That's one of what we categorize as four
distribution channels. We have a pretty sizable US institutional effort, long-standing,
very well-established with the larger consultants. We have about 400 institutional clients
of size in all of the major market segments here, so insurance, sub-advisor, union, fine benefit,
and corporate. That's a pretty effective and long-standing kind of effort for us,
and it's of size. The other one, which is very unique, is our direct business. In our direct
business, we have hundreds of thousands of individual clients that have bought a mutual fund
brokerage account or a 529 plan directly from us. That's truly B2C or Directive Consumer,
and they access our products through an app, a website, or a contact center here in San Antonio.
We have no infield representatives or live meeting representatives. We have our total
contact center here, and that's a unique distribution channel, and that's sizable,
and it's direct to the end consumer. We get great data out of there because we're dealing with the
end buyer. Then I would say our largest sales effort is our US intermediary. We have deep
relationships and deep penetration into the largest US platforms on the retirement side,
and kind of the non-retirement side. The Merrill Lynch's, the Morgan Stanley's, the Rainier James,
the UBS's, the Empowers, the Fidelities, all the retirement consultants and platforms.
We have a major effort there, so we have a large wholesaling force, a large internal sales desk,
we have ETF sales specialists, we have model sales specialists, we have retirement sales
specialists, we have dedicated data and analytics people, we have our own proprietary technology
around, I'd say, data sorting and focusing our salespeople on certain clients. We have a dedicated
registered investment advisor sales force, dedicated national accounts team, marketing team,
so a massive effort there where the size and scale really matters, and so our distribution
in each channel is deep, and I'd say effective and large, but then we have it in really four
channels as well, which I think makes us really unique. I would say we, I'd use this term that
we punch much bigger than our weight, and so that's a big focus, is getting the clients and
servicing clients and meeting the clients with the vehicle and where they want to meet, how they
want to meet. Now one key component of Victory Capital is the fact that it's a publicly traded
company, and rightly or wrongly, many view kind of report card of whether a strategy is working or
not, is a total shareholder return, and David, as you indicated, it's been pretty phenomenal.
I'll perform the peers, number one, total shareholder return in its categories, so clearly
top marks on the report card, but with that, you've been the leader of the firm for quite a
while. Now what kind of are the main characteristics or are the main factors that you attribute
the success of the firm to? You know, I really start off with the culture. When we did our MBO,
we wanted to create an employee-owned and led culture and mindset, and we came out of an
environment where we had no ownership, and I really believe in an investment management firm.
It's a human capital business. Our assets go up and down the elevators every single day,
and I think your best way for success is to have a culture where you put the employees
at the center of decision-making, you put the long-term thinking, and so the culture we've
created around the employees, I think, has been differentiated, and we've kept, you know,
it's not just ownership around a stock or even our products. I would say it's how we go to work
every day, and I use the example of, you know, if you, you know, when you have your own car,
you wash it. When you rent a car, I don't know anybody that, you fill the gas, but I don't even
wash as a car before they return it, and I would say as an employee, you're probably returning
the car dirty with a full gas. As an owner, you're washing the car and you're gassing it up, and
that's how, that's the environment we've tried to create. You know, we've had great success with
growth. Most of the people that work here have increased their, you know, their responsibilities,
they've increased their ability to, you know, to provide for their families from a
compensation perspective, and so we've created a really unique culture. That's the first thing.
I think the second thing is, you know, I think led by our team is we just have an unwavering
kind of desire to just be successful and compete, and our competition is, you know, outside of our
organization with other investment management firms, but it's ultimately, how do you provide the
best performance for your clients? And if you looked at our investment performance, it's at
the top. When you roll all of it up, it's always been at the top, and I think that that's another,
you know, thing is, ultimately, we get paid as an organization for providing investment returns
to our clients. You know, we tell our clients how we're going to manage money, you have to manage
it well, you have to do it, and if you don't, at some point your clients are going to fire you.
And I think that's a big part of it. But we've also had, we have great retention,
and I think, you know, part of the success of our business has also been is, is we have gotten really
smart and much better over the years of recruiting the right kind of people for our culture. And,
you know, I think that that's, I think retention is important, and I think having the people that
fit in your culture. So we might not have the best 700 plus people individually,
but when you put them all together and how they interact as a team, I think we have the best
700 people for our culture that we could possibly, possibly have. As they say, the proof is in the
pudding. Now, David, prior to letting you go, just one last question. As a long-tenured public
company CEO, you know, you did this management buyout, brought the company public and have done
very well as a public company. Any advice for the next generation of business leaders?
Well, I think, foundationally, nothing good comes without hard work and consistency and a
long-term view. And so I think, you know, in today's world where everything has to be immediate,
I think taking a long-term view, understanding that things are built over long periods of time,
at least of anything of value, anything that's built probably quickly isn't going to last.
I think the idea of having a long-term view and decision-making around long-term and working
hard, there's no substitute for that. I think at least as a public company, one of the best skills,
as a public company CEO, one of the best skills you can have is to listen. You get the opportunity
with your shareholders and research analysts to hear a lot of different opinions. And many of them
probably are not good opinions. You have the ability to listen to somebody that you might not
agree with, who maybe was who you meet with every quarter, maybe an analyst that you meet with every
quarter. And every time that person speaks, you totally disagree with them. You think they have no
value at all. But when they speak, you can listen to that person with an open mind and really listen
to what they're saying and get over maybe what your opinion or your bias is. You can be really
smart and successful because most of the times, you're going to get a lot of good input and you're
going to get a lot of good perspective and it'll make you a better decision maker. And so that would
be some advice I'd give a public company. And I think the last thing they have is the public
markets are really tough. And somebody told me this when we were in public is, if you have the
perspective that nobody needs to own your stock at all and understand that every day that nobody
meets you and you have to prove to them why they do, I think that's a good starting point when
you start to interact. Yeah, that's a great point as to the difficulties and opportunities in being
a public company. And with that, David, thanks so much for coming on the show. I encourage investors
to check out the Victory Capital Story. VCTR is the ticker symbol. So David, we wish you the best
of luck in the future. And thanks for coming on the show. Thank you for having me. It's been great.
